top_story: By 31 July, signs that Washington and Israel were preparing strikes on Iranian energy infrastructure were overtaken by a sharper escalation when Iran hit two tankers under U.S. escort in the Strait of Hormuz, pushing the confrontation from signaling into direct pressure on global shipping and energy markets. This sequence raises the risk that any next round of U.S.-Israeli action will target Iran’s economic lifelines, widening the war’s reach from military sites to civilian livelihoods across the Gulf through higher prices, disrupted trade, and heightened insecurity. On the same day, Trump promoted a Gaza deal as a breakthrough, but the unresolved order of Israeli withdrawal and Hamas disarmament exposed how fragile the proposal remains and how little clarity exists for Gazans still waiting for a workable postwar authority. The regional picture is one of simultaneous diplomacy and escalation, with the Hormuz attacks carrying the greater immediate weight because they shorten decision time for leaders and deepen the social and economic shock already spreading across the region.
